title: Dissipation-engineered dual-charger quantum batteries
authors: Yi-jia Yang, Yu-qiang Liu, Zheng Liu, Zhi-Hao Ma, Ming-Xing Luo, Chang-shui Yu
abstract: Suppressing coherent energy backflow while maintaining extractable energy in a stable nonequilibrium state remains a central challenge for quantum energy storage. Here, we introduce a reservoir-engineered dual-charger quantum battery architecture, in which nonequilibrium dissipation is exploited as a control resource to stabilize useful stored energy. A hot-reservoir-coupled driver supplies excitations, while a cold-reservoir-coupled cache biases the resonant three-body transition toward charging and suppresses the dressed-state coherences responsible for energy backflow. This mechanism establishes a population-inverted steady state with finite ergotropy and converts reversible charger--battery exchange into persistent energy storage. For uniformly spaced multilevel batteries, we show that the stored energy and ergotropy scale approximately linearly with the number of accessible levels, while the stored-energy utilization approaches unity. The accompanying stationary heat current provides a thermodynamic signature of the charging regime. Our results demonstrate dissipation engineering as a strategy for achieving stable and scalable quantum energy storage beyond transient coherent charging protocols.
summary: The paper introduces a novel dual-charger quantum battery architecture where controlled dissipation from thermal reservoirs is actively used as a resource. By coupling the battery to hot and cold reservoirs, the authors stabilize a non-equilibrium steady state that prevents energy backflow. This method proves dissipation engineering is a robust strategy for achieving stable and scalable quantum energy storage.
main_problem: The central challenge is stabilizing useful stored energy in a quantum battery while suppressing detrimental coherent energy backflow.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that engineering dissipation via coupled hot/cold reservoirs stabilizes a population-inverted, non-equilibrium steady state with finite ergotropy for scalable quantum energy storage.
method: The analysis uses open-system dynamics described by a Born–Markov–secular master equation to model the interaction between the battery and two reservoir-coupled chargers.
model_or_system: The system is a dual-charger quantum battery (DQB) consisting of an N-level battery coupled to a low-frequency cache and a high-frequency driver, all interacting with thermal reservoirs.
key_observables: Stored energy ($E_B$), ergotropy ($W_B$, extractable work), stored-energy utilization ($\xi_B$), and the stationary heat current ($\dot{Q}_{	ext{ss}}$).
important_parameters: The relative coupling rates ($\kappa_\mu$) and the temperature bias ($\Delta T = T_{C_d} - T_{C_c}$) are key parameters for optimizing performance.
main_assumptions: Assumes weak system–reservoir coupling, short reservoir correlation times (Markov limit), and utilizes a dispersive regime approximation when deriving effective interactions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of charging dynamics between DQB, SQB, and IQB; show time evolution dependence on initial states for DQB; and demonstrate optimization by varying dissipation ratios or temperature bias.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and Hamiltonian, derives the master equation describing open-system dynamics, analyzes steady-state properties using reservoir engineering principles, and concludes by showing scalability metrics like linear scaling of energy with battery levels.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium thermodynamics in quantum systems, providing a concrete mechanism (dissipation engineering) to achieve stable energy storage beyond simple coherent charging protocols, which is highly relevant for AMO physics and open quantum system dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic dual-charger quantum battery (DQB). (a) System setup. A multilevel battery B with level spacing ωB is coupled to two detuned two-level chargers: a driver Cd with frequency ωCd and a cache Cc with frequency ωCc. Each subsystem is connected to an independent thermal reservoir with temperatures TCc < TB < TCd and dissipation rates κCc = κCd ≡κC and κB. (b) Effective three-body interac- tion. Under the resonance condition ωCd = ωCc + ωB, the interaction HCcCdB(t) couples |g, e, n−1⟩and |e, g, n⟩. In the forward process, one driver excitation is converted into one battery excitation and one cache excitation. Parameters are inspired by recent superconducting-circuit experiments...

FIG. 2. Transient charging dynamics of a two-level DQB. (a) Battery ergotropy W ts B and stored-energy utilization ξts B. (b) Transient stored energies of the driver Cd and cache Cc for two dissipation ratios, κB = 10−3κC and κB = 10−1κC. (c) Comparison between the DQB, a single-charger quantum battery (SQB), and an independent-charger quantum battery (IQB) under the same autonomous dissipative setting. The left time window shows oscillatory charging dominated by co- herent exchange, while the right time window shows mono- tonic charging stabilized by dissipation. The shaded regions mark the coherence-dominated (Coh.), coherence–dissipation (Coh.–Diss.), and dissipation-dominated (Diss.)...

FIG. 3. Dependence on the initial charger preparation. Time evolution of (a) stored battery energy EB(t) and (b) ergotropy WB(t) for four initial charger states, with the battery initially in |0⟩B. The preparation |g⟩Cc ⊗|e⟩Cd matches the forward three-body transition and gives the strongest coherent onset, while all initial states relax to the same dissipatively stabilized steady state.

FIG. 4. Dependence on the dissipation ratio. Time evolu- tion of (a) stored battery energy EB(t), (b) ergotropy WB(t), and (c) stored-energy utilization ξB(t) for different dissipa- tion ratios κB/κC, with fixed driver-cache temperature bias. Smaller κB/κC suppresses direct battery relaxation and sta- bilizes larger steady-state ergotropy.

FIG. 5. Dependence on the driver-cache temperature bias. Time evolution of (a) stored battery energy EB(t), (b) er- gotropy WB(t), and (c) stored-energy utilization ξB(t) for dif- ferent temperature biases ∆T = TCd −TCc, with fixed dissipa- tion ratio κB/κC. A positive driver-cache bias favors the for- ward charger-assisted transition and stabilizes a population- inverted battery state.
